symptoms: Our real-time monitoring alerted us to anomalies at approximately 14:01.
The primary node of a highly available Redis cluster became completely unavailable, although the cluster successfully failed over to its secondary.
Some API instances were experiencing Redis connection issues after the failover.
Our API endpoints continued to show abnormal latency after an initial rolling restart.
An expensive API endpoint was receiving a high volume of client requests, degrading overall API performance.
A non-critical Cassandra cluster was experiencing problems under load.
At approximately 15:41, our monitoring showed another anomaly.
Users reported that some community servers appeared offline and that they were having trouble connecting.
A node in our community-server cluster was behaving abnormally.
Some nodes in our session-management cluster were also behaving abnormally.
Later in the incident, our push service experienced a failure.
visible_during_incident.affected_service: Our real-time chat platform, particularly the community-server cluster and its supporting API and session-management services.
visible_during_incident.dependent_impact: Users could not access some community servers and experienced connection problems. Our API performance was degraded, a non-critical Cassandra cluster was affected by high request volume, and our session-management and push services experienced additional problems.
visible_during_incident.scope: A portion of our community servers appeared offline to users. The precise percentage of affected users was not reported. During the later service restart, millions of connected clients needed to reconnect.
visible_during_incident.timing: Initial monitoring anomalies appeared at approximately 14:01 PDT. API issues continued until approximately 14:57, when the API returned to a nominal state. Another anomaly appeared at approximately 15:41, followed by reports of unavailable community servers at 15:42 and additional service problems.
visible_during_incident.trigger: At approximately 14:01, an automatic cloud infrastructure migration occurred involving the primary node of our highly available Redis cluster. The former primary became unavailable, and the cluster failed over to its secondary.
environment: Redis in a highly available primary-secondary cluster
Cloud-hosted infrastructure with automatic instance migrations
Edge caching and an upstream edge network
already_tried: We investigated the initial monitoring anomalies and identified an unavailable Redis primary node.
We confirmed that the Redis cluster had successfully failed over to its secondary, but some API instances were still experiencing connection issues.
We escalated a P1 support ticket to our cloud infrastructure provider.
We investigated the API instances that were not handling Redis failover properly.
We continued investigating abnormal API latency after the initial rolling restart.
When a later monitoring anomaly appeared, we investigated reports of community servers appearing offline.
We identified an abnormally behaving node in the community-server cluster and investigated possible mitigations.
We forcefully removed that node from the service hashring in an attempt to make it decommission itself.
We identified additional misbehaving nodes in the session-management cluster and began investigating them.
When the push service experienced problems, we investigated restoration options and attempted to reduce load by blacklisting traffic that depended on it.

complete_message: Since approximately 15:41 PDT, our real-time chat platform has been showing monitoring anomalies, and users are reporting that some community servers appear offline and that they are having trouble connecting. Earlier, around 14:01 PDT, an automatic cloud infrastructure migration coincided with the loss of a Redis primary node and a failover, followed by API connection issues and abnormal latency. The API had returned to normal before this new disruption, but we are now seeing problems in our community-server and session-management clusters, with a portion of community servers affected and the exact number of impacted users still unknown.

discovered_later.root_cause: The initial disruption began when an automatic cloud infrastructure migration caused the primary node of a highly available Redis cluster to become unavailable. Although the cluster correctly failed over to its secondary, a previously known bug in how API instances handled Redis failover caused significant API degradation. This disruption also exposed an incorrectly configured edge caching rule for an expensive API endpoint, leading clients to make excessive requests and overloading a non-critical Cassandra cluster. The initial disruption was followed by failures in the real-time infrastructure: nodes in other services entered abnormal states, eventually ran out of memory, and contributed to a cascading system failure. The exact mechanism connecting the initial API disruption to the wider cascading failure was not determined. A later investigation identified potential flaws in a library used by an affected service, but their precise role in the cascade remained uncertain.
fix: We performed an initial rolling restart of all API instances to address Redis connection issues.
We corrected the misconfigured edge caching rule affecting the expensive API endpoint.
We disabled the problematic API endpoint at the upstream edge network.
We recovered the overloaded Cassandra cluster and restored its normal operation.
We performed another rolling restart of all API instances to address latency associated with the Cassandra cluster problems.
We forcefully restarted the misbehaving community-server node, which succeeded.
When additional services began failing, we initiated a full service restart to reset invalid states across the affected components.
We investigated the push service failure and attempted to reduce dependent traffic while recovery was underway.
We corrected an improperly configured API setting that was needed to allow users to reconnect quickly and safely.
We monitored and addressed remaining instabilities as the platform recovered, with full service restored at approximately 16:52 PDT.
prevention: Increase the priority of fixing the known Redis failover handling bug so individual node failures do not cause major API degradation.
Improve the behavior of the expensive API route so similar failures do not degrade other services.
Add monitoring for signals associated with the cascading failure to provide earlier warnings and more time for investigation.
Continue improving reliability and failure handling across the affected services.
Investigate potential flaws in a library used by an affected service and roll out an update believed to address those problems, while continuing to investigate the unresolved failure mechanism.
discovered_later.changes: During the incident, we corrected the edge caching configuration, disabled the problematic API endpoint at the upstream edge network, and corrected the API setting required for safe and rapid client reconnection. Afterward, we modified the problematic route's behavior to handle similar errors without degrading other services and added monitoring for signals associated with cascading failures. A library update was also being prepared based on subsequent investigation, but its effectiveness had not yet been confirmed.
